questions.question: Define a contour line and the contour interval, state the four rules of contour lines, and give the contour interval on a 1:50 000 topographic map and a 1:10 000 orthophoto map.
questions.expected_answer: A contour line joins points of equal height above mean sea level. The contour interval is the constant height difference between neighbouring contours: 20 m on the 1:50 000 map and 5 m on the 1:10 000 orthophoto. Rules: contours join points of the same height; they never cross or split (they merge only at a vertical cliff); every contour closes on itself, on or beyond the sheet; the innermost closed loops mark summits.

questions.question: Explain how contour spacing shows steep, gentle, convex and concave slopes, and explain why roads and settlements are usually found on gentle slopes.
questions.expected_answer: Close spacing shows a steep slope, wide spacing a gentle slope and no contours flat land. Close at the bottom and wide at the top shows a convex slope; wide at the bottom and close at the top shows a concave slope; even spacing shows a uniform slope. Roads, railways and settlements are on gentle slopes because construction and travel are easier, cheaper and safer, and steep land is harder to build on and more prone to erosion.

questions.question: Calculate the gradient between a spot height of 1 420 m and a trig station of 1 680 m that are 4 cm apart on a 1:50 000 map, showing the formula and every step.
questions.expected_answer: Gradient = VI / HE. VI = 1 680 - 1 420 = 260 m. HE = 4 cm x 50 000 = 200 000 cm = 2 000 m. Gradient = 260 / 2 000 = 1 : (2 000 / 260) = 1:7,7. For every 1 m rise, 7,7 m is travelled horizontally.
